specPoints.text: describe nuclear fusion as the creation of larger nuclei resulting in a loss of mass from smaller nuclei, accompanied by a release of energy
explain the difference between nuclear fusion and nuclear fission

primer.text: Fusion builds up: two light nuclei merge into a heavier one, and a sliver of mass converts into a colossal release of energy. Stars fuse hydrogen into helium; fission instead breaks heavy nuclei apart in reactors — the two processes differ in fuel, products, location and the conditions they demand.

lessons.title: The fusion process
lessons.opening: Nuclear fusion joins two light nuclei into one heavier nucleus. In most stars hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, and the energy released is enormous because a tiny fraction of the particles' mass is converted into energy — fusing 1 kg of hydrogen matches burning about ten million kilograms of coal.
keyPoints: Fusion joins two light nuclei into one heavier nucleus.
Stars fuse hydrogen into helium and release huge amounts of energy.
The energy appears because a small part of the mass is converted into energy.
Fusion demands extremely high temperatures to keep running.
1 kg of hydrogen fused matches burning about ten million kilograms of coal.

low.restatement: Fusion: two light nuclei merge, a speck of mass turns into energy.
low.analogy: Two raindrops merging into one bigger drop — the join releases a splash.
low.examPointer: Remember the direction: fusion builds up from small nuclei; fission breaks down from large ones.

medium.restatement: Mass–energy conversion powers fusion: the product nucleus carries slightly less mass than its two parents, and the deficit is released as energy.
medium.analogy: Packing two suitcases into one smaller case — the squeezed-out space appears as the burst of energy.
medium.examPointer: The coal equivalence is an order-of-magnitude comparison; never present it as an exact conversion.

check.stem: Fusion produces a larger nucleus by…

options.explanation: Two light nuclei merge into one heavier nucleus.

options.text: splitting one large nucleus into two
options.explanation: That is fission.
Electrons are irrelevant to nuclear fusion.
Alpha emission is a decay mode, not fusion.

check.stem: Which fuel do most stars fuse?

options.explanation: Hydrogen fusion to helium powers most stars.
Uranium is a fission fuel, not a stellar fusion fuel.
Plutonium belongs to reactors, not stars.
That is a combustion chemical, not a nuclear fuel.

check.stem: Where does the energy released in fusion come from?

options.text: a small part of the particles' mass converted into energy
options.explanation: The fused nucleus has slightly less mass; the difference appears as energy.
Nuclei do not rub against each other.
Fusion is nuclear, not chemical.
Volume change is not the energy source.

check.stem: Fusing 1 kg of hydrogen releases about as much energy as burning…

options.explanation: The of-record equivalence is roughly 10,000,000 kg of coal.
That is a thousandfold underestimate.
Fusion's yield dwarfs chemical burning.
That overstates the equivalence a hundredfold.

check.stem: Why is fusion hard to sustain on Earth?

options.text: it demands extremely high temperatures that are hard to reach and hold
options.explanation: Only extreme heat lets light nuclei overcome their repulsion.

options.text: because hydrogen is a rare element
options.explanation: Hydrogen is abundant.

options.text: because the waste stays dangerous for millennia
options.explanation: Fusion produces no long-lived waste products.

options.text: because it releases too little energy
options.explanation: Fusion's energy release is enormous.

check.modelAnswer: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to make a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.

check.stem: State what most stars fuse and what it becomes.
check.modelAnswer: Stars fuse hydrogen nuclei into helium, releasing energy.

check.stem: Explain how merging lighter nuclei can release energy at all.
check.modelAnswer: The nucleus built by fusion has slightly less mass than the two nuclei that formed it; that missing mass is converted into energy, which is why fusion releases such enormous power.

check.stem: A fusion trial fuses 3 kg of hydrogen. Using the coal equivalence, how many kilograms of coal give the same energy?
check.modelAnswer: 1 kg of hydrogen fused matches about 10,000,000 kg of coal, so 3 kg matches 3 × 10,000,000 = 30,000,000 kg of coal.

lessons.title: Fusion versus fission
lessons.opening: The two nuclear energy processes point in opposite directions. Fusion joins small nuclei such as hydrogen and runs in stars; fission splits large nuclei such as uranium and runs in reactors. Fusion's products are usually stable, its hydrogen fuel is abundant in water, and it leaves no long-lived waste — but its conditions are far harder to achieve on Earth.
keyPoints: Fusion joins small nuclei such as hydrogen; fission splits large nuclei such as uranium.
Fusion happens in stars; fission runs in nuclear reactors on Earth.
Fusion's products are usually stable; fission leaves radioactive daughters plus neutrons.
Fusion needs very high temperatures and pressures; fission needs thermal neutrons to induce it.
Fusion fuel from water is more abundant than fissile ore, and fusion leaves no long-lived waste.

low.restatement: Fusion = join small nuclei (stars); fission = split large nuclei (reactors).
low.analogy: Construction versus demolition: fusion welds bricks together, fission knocks a building into two unstable halves.
low.examPointer: Comparison tables reward precision: fuel, location, products and conditions are the four rows to memorise.

medium.restatement: Every contrast line pairs with its mirror: hydrogen/uranium, stars/reactors, stable/radioactive products, heat+pressure/thermal neutrons.
medium.analogy: Two opposite weather systems: one builds a cloud up, the other tears it apart — same sky, opposite dynamics.
medium.examPointer: Per-kilogram energy and waste longevity are the two standard fusion advantage marks; conditions difficulty is the standard disadvantage.

check.stem: Which comparison of the two processes is correct?

options.text: fusion joins small nuclei while fission splits large ones
options.explanation: Build-up versus break-down is the core contrast.

options.text: fusion splits large nuclei while fission joins small ones
options.explanation: The two processes are swapped.
Only fusion joins.
Only fission splits.

check.stem: Which product pattern follows each process?

options.text: fusion usually makes stable larger nuclei; fission makes radioactive daughters and neutrons
options.explanation: Fission fragments stay unstable; fusion products tend to be stable.

options.text: fusion makes radioactive waste while fission makes stable nuclei
options.explanation: The patterns are reversed.
Neutrons accompany fission; fusion products are nuclei.
Both transform nuclei — that is their point.

check.stem: Where does each process occur today?

options.text: fusion in stars, fission in power reactors
options.explanation: Stellar cores fuse; terrestrial reactors fission.
Fusion reactors are not yet commercially viable.
Fission is a reactor process.

options.text: fusion in reactors, fission in stars
options.explanation: Both locations are swapped.

check.stem: What does fission require that fusion does not?

options.text: thermal neutrons to induce the split
options.explanation: Fission needs a neutron capture; fusion needs extreme heat and pressure.
That is fusion's demand, not fission's.
Hydrogen fuels fusion.
Stellar pressure is a fusion condition.

check.stem: Which is an advantage of future fusion reactors over fission reactors?

options.text: their hydrogen fuel is abundant and no long-lived waste is produced
options.explanation: Water supplies the isotopes, and the products are not long-lived waste.

options.text: they need uranium and plutonium ore
options.explanation: Those are fission fuels.
Fusion avoids long-lived waste.
Fusion needs extreme temperatures.

check.stem: State one difference between the nuclei used in fusion and in fission.
check.modelAnswer: Fusion uses small nuclei such as hydrogen; fission uses large nuclei such as uranium.

check.stem: State what fission produces that fusion does not.
check.modelAnswer: Fission produces radioactive daughter nuclei and two or three neutrons.

check.stem: Explain why fusion fuel is considered more abundant than fission fuel.
check.modelAnswer: Fusion burns isotopes of hydrogen that can be taken from water, while fission depends on uranium and plutonium ores that are far scarcer to mine.

check.stem: A student claims fission products are safe because they are stable. Correct the claim.
check.modelAnswer: It is fusion that usually makes stable larger nuclei; fission daughters are usually unstable and radioactive, which is why reactor waste needs careful handling.

glossary.definition: Joining of two light nuclei into a heavier nucleus, converting a little mass into energy.
Splitting of a large nucleus into smaller radioactive daughters plus neutrons.
The larger nucleus built when hydrogen isotopes fuse in stars.
